paper_title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: AI-driven game generation holds the potential to make game development more accessible and efficient, enabling broader range of creators to transform their ideas into interactive experiences. Recent advances in large language models have further enabled coding agents to generate playable games and modify existing game projects from natural language instructions Wang et al. [2023] Sudhakaran et al. [2023]. However, game creation often begins with inspiration from novels, photographs, films, gameplay videos, or personal experiences rather than explicit specifications. To this end, agents must identify transferable mechanisms, visual characteristics, entities, and relationships from reference content, and integrate them into coherent game worlds, gameplay mechanics, and narratives while 1 GameAnything 2 Figure 1. GameAnything: From Any Inspiration to Playable Game Worlds. GameAnything transforms diverse inspirations, including films, game trailers, real-world footage, images, and literature, into playable game extensions. Middle: illustrates the agentic construction pipeline alongside benchmark statistics and model performance. Bottom: showcases representative game extensions across diverse gaming environments. GameAnything 3 preserving the functionality of the original game. For example, adapting tennis match into an existing game requires translating its rules and interactions into playable mechanics. Achieving this requires both accurate understanding of diverse reference materials and reliable game development capabilities. Existing game development systems and evaluation benchmarks primarily focus on game generation from textual specifications or design documents Luo et al. [2026], Dong et al. [2026], Chen et al. [2026], feature implementation and repair in existing projects Chi et al. [2026], Chen et al. [2026], and game modding from natural language requests Ku et al. [2026]. However, these systems and benchmarks have not systematically addressed how diverse external references can be understood and adapted into playable game content, including their underlying mechanisms, visual characteristics, and relationships. Moreover, existing evaluation benchmarks largely rely on scripted action replay and runtime probes to verify predefined behaviors, providing limited insight into actual gameplay experiences from players perspective. More comprehensive game development systems and evaluation benchmarks are therefore needed to support and assess inspiration-driven content adaptation and its coherent integration into playable games, better reflecting real-world game development needs and player experiences. To address these limitations, we introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms diverse human inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through autonomous and iterative development. GameAnything establishes continuous development loop in which coding agents interpret reference content and implement game modifications, while an independent critic autonomously playtests the resulting games to identify unmet requirements, functional failures, and regressions. These findings are incorporated into persistent development state to guide subsequent revisions, with sparse human feedback steering high-level creative decisions. Beyond individual tasks, GameAnything consolidates verified development experience into reusable memory, allowing subsequent development cycles to benefit from previous experience. Inspired by the experienceguided improvement mechanism of RSIAgent [Zhu et al., 2026a], this design supports recursive self-improvement across game versions and tasks. With modular interfaces for different coding agents and game environments, GameAnything further serves as general evaluation framework for systematically assessing inspiration-driven game development, development reliability, and gameplay quality. We further introduce GameAnything-Bench, benchmark for systematically evaluating how coding agents understand multimodal references and transform their content into playable extensions of existing games. The benchmark organizes tasks into three categories based on their primary creation objectives: Scene & World, Mechanics & Behavior, and Narrative & Event, covering diverse references including text, images, videos, and their combinations. To support reproducible evaluation across diverse gaming environments, GameAnything-Bench includes core track built on open-source games and separate commercial game track for broader assessment. For evaluation, the benchmark combines runtime probes, scripted action replay, and exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Unlike evaluations limited to predefined test trajectories, this approach enables the discovery of unexpected failures and gameplay inconsistencies, providing more comprehensive assessment of game development capabilities from players perspective. We evaluate nine coding agent configurations on GameAnything-Bench and uncover three key findings. First, current agents can realize reference-grounded content and generally preserve existing games, but struggle to implement fully playable interactions and precise edits. Second, multimodal GameAnything 4 references substantially improve content and visual fidelity, while agent capabilities vary sharply. Claude Fable 5.2 Anthropic [2026b] leads Construction by 24.9 points, whereas DeepSeek V4.1 Flash DeepSeek-AI [2026] offers the strongest open-weight performance at substantially lower cost. Most agents perform best on image references, but Kimi K3 Kimi Team [2026] and Qwen3.8Max Alibaba Cloud [2026b] exhibit relative strengths on hybrid and video inputs, respectively. Third, iterative refinement reveals distinct improvement trajectories across agents. Qwen3.8-Flash Alibaba Cloud [2026a] gains only 0.8 Construction points after one round but 14.8 after three, while refined DeepSeek V4.1 Flash nearly matches native Claude Sonnet 5.5 Anthropic [2026c] at comparable development cost.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Benchmarking game generation. Recent benchmarks increasingly focus on end-to-end game generation, which requires coding agents to build complete playable games from scratch. V-GameGym Zhang et al. [2026] curates Pygame tasks from real repositories and scores generated code, screenshots, and gameplay videos with LLM/MLLM judges. OpenGame-Bench Jiang et al. [2026] evaluates browser game generation by grading rendered visuals with VLM. PlaytestArena Huang et al. [2026] instead pairs browser-game prompts with behavioral rubrics verified by an autonomous GUI playtesting agent. GameCraft-Bench Luo et al. [2026] validates complete Godot projects by replaying agent-submitted interaction traces. CEGame-Bench Dong et al. [2026] likewise builds new games and verifies them with runtime probes and action replay. Movie2Game-Bench Xie et al. [2026] replaces the text description with full film and, alongside general game quality and agent playtesting, scores how much film-specific content survives into player interaction, leaving the game genre and design to the agent. In contrast, GameAnything-Bench moves beyond blank-canvas generation to evaluate cross-world transfer and preservation-aware editing, challenging agents to adapt multimodal references into existing games native mechanics and iteratively modify them without breaking intact content. Game editing. More closely related are benchmarks grounded in existing game repositories. GameDevBench Chi et al. [2026] turns Godot tutorials into feature-implementation tasks and verifies them with engine-side tests. SWE-Game Chen et al. [2026] combines construction tasks, which build game from brief or design document, with skeleton-completion, repair, and porting tasks on executable reference games, and scores both fault restoration and preservation of unaffected behavior. IGMBench Ku et al. [2026] frames Minecraft and Terraria modding as world editing at increasing intervention depth, graded by executable state, behavioral, and regression checks. In these benchmarks, the target change is specified by text request or by reference version of the same game. GameAnything-Bench instead requires agents to transfer content from external multimodal references into different existing game as new mod. It covers both construction and editing, and evaluates them by combining preservation checks, runtime probes, action replay, and agent playtesting  (Table 1)  . Simulated environment generation. RobotAgentBench [Mao et al., 2026] uses 50 simulated household layouts to evaluate task discovery, manipulation, and recovery from failures. In game development, most benchmarks target single engine or modding framework. V-GameGym Zhang et al. [2026] targets Pygame, while OpenGame-Bench Jiang et al. [2026] and PlaytestArena Huang et al. [2026] target browser games. GameDevBench Chi et al. [2026], GameCraft-Bench Luo et al. GameAnything 5 Table 1. Comparison with existing game development benchmarks.

sections.content: Task Formulation. We study how coding agents transfer ideas and experiences from multimodal references into existing games, and further develop them into new playable worlds, mechanics, and narratives. Given multimodal references 𝑋, user instruction 𝑢, and target game 𝐺, coding agent develops game modification 𝑀. The modification includes code, assets, and configurations needed to extend the target game. Unlike game generation from scratch, the agent must understand and work with the existing games completed and comples projects, and conduct further development in it without destroying original functions. Rather than simply reproducing the references, agents must identify and transfer their underlying mechanisms, visual characteristics, and relationships, then build upon them to create new playable content in the target game. sections.title: 4 GameAnything
sections.content: GameAnything extends coding agents from one-time generation to iterative game development grounded in gameplay evidence. Given multimodal references 𝑅, user instruction 𝐼, and game project 𝑃𝑡, the framework iteratively updates the project: Δ𝑡 𝜋builder( 𝑅, 𝐼, 𝑃𝑡, 𝑆𝑡, M), 𝑃𝑡+1 = Apply(𝑃𝑡, Δ𝑡). (3) Here, 𝑆𝑡 maintains verified development progress, while stores reusable experience from previous tasks. The framework combines two complementary processes: autonomous playtesting and verification within each task, and experience accumulation across tasks.

sections.title: 4.1 Evidence-Grounded Iterative Development
sections.content: Persistent Development State. GameAnything maintains structured development state 𝑆𝑡 that tracks task requirements, completion status, supporting evidence, and unresolved issues: 𝑆𝑡 = (Q, 𝝈𝑡, E𝑡, K𝑡), (4) where denotes task requirements, 𝝈𝑡 records their status, E𝑡 stores supporting evidence, and K𝑡 maintains recheck list. Each requirement is tracked as todo, partial, done, broken, or regressed. The builder records development progress, while an independent playtester verifies completion through gameplay evidence. Previously satisfied requirements that fail in subsequent rounds are marked as regressions and added to the recheck list. The state carries verified progress and unresolved issues between rounds, much like the verifier-backed checkpoints in StructAgent [Wu et al., 2026b]. Autonomous Playtesting and Verification. At each round, the builder implements or revises the game according to the current development state. It then launches the updated project 𝑃𝑡+1 and performs gameplay interactions to collect an observation trace 𝜏𝑡. An independent playtester examines the resulting evidence against the user instruction and reference materials: 𝜏𝑡 𝜋play ( 𝑃𝑡+1, 𝐼, 𝑆𝑡), 𝑣𝑡 𝜋verify ( 𝑅, 𝐼, 𝑃𝑡+1, 𝑆𝑡, 𝜏𝑡). (5) Here, 𝑣𝑡 identifies verified requirements, remaining issues, and regressions. The verification results update the development state: 𝑆𝑡+1 = Update(𝑆𝑡, 𝜏𝑡, 𝑣𝑡). (6) The updated state guides the next revision, and the process continues until the requirements are verified or the development budget is exhausted. This grounds iterative improvement in actual gameplay rather than code inspection alone. Appendix shows this process on three projects. GameAnything 7 Figure 2. Overview of GameAnything. sections.title: 4.3 Interactive Platform and Extensibility
sections.content: User-Guided Game Creation. GameAnything provides local web interface that allows users to transform personal memories, stories, images, and videos into playable content without writing code. Users provide multimodal references and creative goals, while the platform presents interactive cards to clarify important design choices, such as characters, locations, visual styles, and gameplay mechanics. After each development cycle, users can review recorded gameplay and provide feedback on specific video frames or image regions. The platform converts this feedback into actionable development requirements and verifies subsequent modifications through corresponding gameplay views. This enables users to guide creative decisions and progressively refine their games through natural interaction; Appendix describes the interface and workflow in detail. Extensible Game and Agent Integration. GameAnything supports heterogeneous game engines and modding ecosystems through modular game adapters that provide interfaces for building, installing, launching, and interacting with games. New games can be integrated through standardized configurations, adapters, and validation tests. The platform also supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code [Anthropic, 2026a], Codex [OpenAI, 2026a], Gemini CLI [Google, 2026], and OpenCode [Anomaly, 2026], allowing users to work with their preferred agent configurations. Development can run locally or in isolated server environments. User materials are managed locally, external model access requires authorization, and game saves are backed up before modifications are installed. Together, these capabilities provide an accessible and extensible platform for creating and continuously refining content in existing games.

sections.title: 5.1 Task Design
sections.content: Task Taxonomy We organize GameAnything-Bench around three fundamental dimensions of reference-to-game adaptation objective: Scene & World Adaptation transfers the visual and spatial structure of places, including objects, landmarks, layouts, and environmental styles. Mechanics & Behavior Adaptation distills underlying rules, motion dynamics, and interaction patterns into executable gameplay. Narrative & Event Adaptation grounds character relationships and causal event sequences into interactive experiences. Crucially, tasks require visual and interactive grounding rather than surface-level visual replication: agents must abstract transferable principles and re-express them through the target games native affordances during construction, while executing targeted modifications without disrupting unspecified game systems during editing. Input Modalities and Task Settings. In real-world game development, creative ideas often draw on multimodal references, while user requests involve both creating and modifying game content. To reflect this diversity, we consider four input modalities and two task settings. For input modalities, GameAnything 9 Figure 3. Overview of GameAnything-Bench. The left panel shows the distribution of 205 tasks across Construction and Editing, task categories, and input modalities. The right panel illustrates the benchmark construction pipeline, where multimodal references undergo information extraction, model cross-review, and human validation to produce 125 Construction tasks. Validated Construction checkpoints further support 80 Editing tasks covering appearance, content and structure, and behavior and flow. we include text, image, video, and hybrid references. Different modalities provide complementary information about visual appearance, mechanisms, and narratives, while hybrid tasks require agents to integrate information across modalities into coherent playable content. For task settings, Construction requires agents to create new playable content in an existing game based on the provided references. Editing requires agents to modify existing playable content according to specific user requests while preserving unrelated content and functionality. Both settings evaluate the ability to translate multimodal inspirations into playable game content. Target Game Selection. We select target games based on diversity, adaptation feasibility, and reproducibility. The selected games span different genres and interaction mechanisms, allowing us to evaluate adaptation across heterogeneous environments. When pairing references with target games, we ensure that each game can meaningfully realize the reference content through its mechanics and modding interfaces. We also avoid sourcetarget pairs that allow direct replication without substantive adaptation. Our core benchmark uses open-source games to enable reproducible execution and evaluation, while separate commercial-game track assesses generalization to commercial games. Further details on game selection and reference-to-game matching criteria are provided in Appendix B.1.

sections.title: 5.2 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Reference Collection and Annotation. We curate diverse multimodal references, including fictions, photographs, manga, film clips, sports footage, gameplay recordings, and travel videos, etc. For video references, we first remove duplicates and extract timestamped clips, keyframes, and transcripts. Then we perform two independent annotation passes to identify transferable content, including mechanisms, entities and their properties, and spatial, temporal, and causal relations. Each annotation is grounded GameAnything 10 in evidence from the original reference. Based on these annotations, we manually select representative references, assign task categories, and match them to target games, considering adaptation potential, diversity, and evaluation feasibility. We extend the same annotation scheme to image and text references, grounding annotations in specific image regions or text passages. More details about reference sources and annotation process can be found in Appendix B.2. Task Construction. Each task consists of reference materials, target game, an agent-visible instruction, and hidden evaluation rubrics. Editing tasks additionally provide validated game checkpoint containing existing playable content. To align task instructions with evaluation criteria, we adopt rubric-first construction process. We define rubrics for content, functionality, visual presentation, and preservation of the host games character, with criteria tailored to Construction and Editing. Each rubric item includes supporting evidence and scoring anchors. We first calibrate the authoring guidelines through multiple rounds of model generation and human feedback on pilot tasks. For large-scale construction, all rubrics undergo independent model cross-review and multiple rounds of human revision before finalization. We then derive instructions by grouping rubrics into broader requirements, and additionally include explicit user requests to preserve, specify, and modify content. Further details are provided in Appendix B.3. Quality Control and Benchmark Statistics. We apply several quality checks to ensure task validity and evaluation reliability. We verify that rubric items are grounded in reference evidence or explicit requirements, exclude incidental details that do not define the intended experience, and review every task before finalization. We also validate game capability probes on unmodified and deliberately corrupted game instances to check executability and host functionality. Further details are provided in Appendix B.3 and Appendix C.1. GameAnything-Bench contains 205 tasks across 14 target games, comprising 125 Construction and 80 Editing tasks. The open-source core includes 77 Construction tasks across nine games and 64 Editing tasks on six of them, while the commercial track includes 48 Construction tasks across five games and 16 Editing tasks across two of them. Construction covers text, image, video, and hybrid references, while Editing spans appearance, content and structure, and behavior and flow modifications. Full distributions are provided in Tables A7 and A8.

sections.title: 5.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Evaluation Dimensions. Successful game development requires both creating new playable content from multimodal references and precisely modifying existing content. We therefore evaluate two complementary capabilities: Construction and Editing. For Construction, Content assesses whether the required entities, properties, structures, and relations are correctly realized, Functions & Playability evaluates whether the created content is functional, interactive, and playable, and Visual & Presentation measures visual fidelity, spatial appearance, and overall presentation quality. For Editing, Edit Success assesses whether the requested change is correctly realized in the game, and Preservation whether content and functions that the edit should not touch remain as they were in the initial checkpoint. Both settings share Host Fidelity, which assesses whether the result is built on and played through the target game, using its world, avatar and controls, systems, and look, rather than replacement that merely runs inside it. GameAnything 11 Evidence Grounded Agentic Evaluation. Creative game development allows multiple valid implementations, making fixed tests and static visual evaluation insufficient to fully assess interactive correctness. We therefore combine rubric based evaluation with gameplay replay and independent agentic playtesting. Automated probes act as gate that checks whether the original game still runs and remains present after modification. Gameplay replay executes action traces submitted by the development agent to verify the implemented features. Independent agentic playtesting further explores the game beyond these traces, assessing whether the content can be discovered and experienced through normal gameplay. Visual evaluation compares captured screenshots against reference grounded rubrics. For Editing, we additionally compare the modified game with its initial checkpoint to verify targeted changes and preservation of unrelated content. Further details are provided in Appendix C.2; agreement with human judgments and the contribution of each evidence source are analyzed in Appendices H.1 and H.2. Scoring Rubrics. Each rubric item is scored as 0, 0.5, or 1, and scores are aggregated within each evaluation dimension. Construction Overall combines content, functionality, visual quality, and host fidelity, while Editing Overall prioritizes edit success with penalties for unintended changes and loss of host fidelity. Submissions that fail the executability gate receive zero. Detailed scoring rules are provided in Appendix C.3, and the stability of the scores across repeated evaluations in Appendix H.3.

sections.title: 6.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Coding Agents. We evaluate nine coding-agent configurations using Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode. The backbone models are Claude Fable 5.2 [Anthropic, 2026b], Claude Sonnet 5.5 [Anthropic, 2026c], GPT-5.6 Sol [OpenAI, 2026b], Gemini 3.8 Flash [Google DeepMind, 2026], GLM5.3-Flash [Z.ai, 2026, GLM-5 Team et al., 2026], Qwen3.8-Max [Alibaba Cloud, 2026b], Qwen3.8Flash [Alibaba Cloud, 2026a], Kimi K3 [Kimi Team, 2026], and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [DeepSeek-AI, 2026]. Each model and its native harness is complete agent system. We retain the default prompts, tools, and reasoning settings of each harness without model-specific tuning. All agents receive identical task instructions, reference materials, and game development interfaces, with the same initial state for each task. Each native agent performs one autonomous attempt with development budget of 120 minutes. We further evaluate iterative refinement with one additional round for eight configurations and three rounds for three selected configurations. Each round provides critic feedback based on gameplay replay, followed by 60 minutes of revision by the same coding agent with lessons retrieved from experience memory. The first Construction round on ten of the fourteen games (98 of 125 tasks) was run before experience memory was added and used 40 minutes without lessons; all later rounds and all Editing rounds use the full setting. Detailed configurations and execution settings are provided in Appendix D.1. Evaluation. We evaluate all submissions independently of the development agents and refinement critics using consistent evaluation protocol. Claude Sonnet 5.5 serves as the judge for replay verification, playtest verification, visual assessment, and adjudication. sections.title: 6.2 Main Results
sections.content: Turning multimodal inspirations into playable content remains challenging. Table 2 reveals substantial capability gaps among current coding agents. Claude Fable 5.2 achieves the highest Construction Overall of 84.1, while the second-best agent reaches only 59.2 and five of the nine agents score below 40. Moreover, across all evaluated agents, Content scores are higher than Functions & Playability scores, suggesting that creating the requested content is easier than making it fully functional and playable. These findings highlight the difficulty of transforming multimodal references into meaningful, interactive experiences within existing games. Editing failures arise primarily from incomplete changes. Coding agents generally preserve existing game content but struggle to implement the requested modifications accurately. As shown in Table 2, Preservation exceeds 94 across all nine agents, while Edit Success ranges from only 62.6 to 87.4. These results indicate that maintaining the original game is not the primary difficulty in editing. Instead, reliably realizing targeted changes remains major challenge. Iterative development can substantially improve initial game quality. Native coding agents leave considerable room for further improvement. As shown in Table A24, single refinement round raises both Construction and Editing scores for all eight evaluated configurations; 11 of these 16 gains have 95% confidence interval that excludes zero (Table A18). Three rounds further increase Construction scores by 7.6 to 14.8 points for the selected agents. Notably, Qwen3.8-Flash gains only 0.8 points after the first round but 14.8 points after three rounds, suggesting that limited early progress does not necessarily imply diminishing potential for further development. sections.title: 7.1 Iterative Refinement and Efficiency
sections.content: Small initial improvements can be followed by substantial gains in later refinement rounds. As shown in Figure 4, Qwen3.8-Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash improve Construction by only 0.8 and 1.1 points after the first round, neither of which is statistically significant. After three rounds, however, their cumulative gains reach 14.8 and 7.6 points, both with confidence intervals excluding zero. Editing exhibits different improvement patterns (Table A24), with DeepSeek obtaining most of its gains in the first round while Qwen3.8-Flash continues improving in later rounds. These findings suggest that limited early progress does not necessarily indicate that further refinement has little value. RSIGame [Wu et al., 2026a] demonstrates the benefits of autonomous game refinement while highlighting the importance of detecting improvement saturation and regression. Our results reveal further tradeoff between continued refinement and starting with stronger coding agent. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reaches 59.1 Construction Overall after three rounds at $1.72 per task, approaching native Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 59.2 and $1.84. However, Qwen3.8-Flash reaches only 50.0 after three rounds at $1.90, still below native DeepSeek at 51.4 and $0.26. Thus, substantial improvements over an agents initial performance do not necessarily translate into better cost efficiency than using stronger agent directly. These comparisons concern development cost rather than matched execution time, and the observed gains reflect additional development time alongside critic feedback and experience memory.

sections.title: 7.2 Multimodal Reference Understanding and Capability Diversity
sections.content: Multimodal references provide information that task instructions alone cannot capture. To examine their contribution, we remove the references from Construction tasks while keeping the instructions and evaluation unchanged (Appendix G.2). As shown in Figure 5 (a), removing references reduces Claude Sonnet 5.5s Overall score by 7.1 points under matched harness settings. The decline is concentrated in Content and Visual & Presentation, with the latter dropping by 14.9 points, while Functions & Playability shows no clear change. This indicates that reference materials are particularly GameAnything 14 Figure 5. Multimodal reference contributions and capability profiles. (a) The score gain from providing references over instruction-only inputs for Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 40-task subset, with paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. (b) Each native agents deviation from its own Construction Overall across input modalities; diamonds indicate the mean over nine agents. (c) Construction Overall of each native agent across input modalities and task categories; the orange dashed curve denotes the mean over nine agents. Exact scores and task counts are provided in Table A23. important for realizing the intended content and visual characteristics. Different input modalities also reveal distinct agent capabilities. As shown in Figure 5 (b), image tasks achieve the highest mean Construction score across the nine agents and are the best-performing modality for seven of them. However, this pattern is not universal. Kimi K3 performs best on hybrid references, while Qwen3.8-Max achieves its highest score on video tasks. These differences reveal model-specific strengths that are obscured by aggregate performance and motivate evaluating coding agents across diverse reference modalities. Agent performance also varies across task categories. As shown in Figure 5 (c), the Qwen models perform relatively better on Mechanics & Behavior tasks, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash achieve their highest scores on Narrative & Event tasks. The exact scores in Table A23 further illustrate these differences across models and task categories.

sections.title: 7.3 Editing Failure Modes
sections.content: Behavioral edits are the most difficult to implement without disrupting existing gameplay. As shown in Figure 6, Behavior & Flow edits have the lowest Edit Success of 66.3, compared with 73.3 for Appearance, and substantially higher rate of collateral damage of 14.3% versus 2.1%. This pattern is consistent across agents. Eight of the nine agents achieve lower Edit Success on behavioral edits, and all nine show lower Preservation. These findings highlight the difficulty of modifying gameplay behavior while keeping surrounding functionality intact. GameAnything 15 Figure 6. Editing failure modes. Fractions of edits that do not achieve the requested change and edits that achieve it but damage unrelated content. The left panel groups results by agent, and the right panel by edit class. The thresholds are Edit Success below 0.5 for missed edits and Edit Success at least 0.5 with Preservation below 0.9 for collateral damage. Figure 7. Reliability of agentic evaluation. The left panel compares the Full evaluator with human judgments on 40 submissions. The right panel reports mean absolute error and bias across evaluation settings, with 95% bootstrap intervals for bias. Bias is the evaluator score minus the human score. Structural edits reveal different failure pattern. Content & Structure edits achieve nearly the same Edit Success as Appearance edits, with scores of 73.0 and 73.3, respectively. However, their Preservation drops from 98.7 to 94.5, indicating greater risk of unintended changes to existing content. This distinction suggests that structural modifications can satisfy the requested change while compromising other parts of the game, revealing limitations that Edit Success alone cannot capture.

sections.title: 7.4 Reliability of Agentic Evaluation
sections.content: Agentic evaluation closely aligns with human judgments and remains stable across repeated runs. As shown in Figure 7, the Full evaluator achieves Pearson correlation of 𝑟 = 0.87 on 40 human-labeled submissions and exactly reproduces the human ranking of six agent models. Compared with the Lite evaluator, independent playtesting and adjudication reduce scoring error and mitigate conservative scoring bias, while maintaining the same correlation with human judgments. Repeated Full evaluations on 47 submissions further demonstrate strong consistency, with an intraclass correlation of 0.93. Additional analyses of evaluator stability and playtesting budget, and of judges from other model families, are provided in Appendices H.3 and H.4. GameAnything

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: 16 In this work, we introduced GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform for transforming diverse human inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through autonomous and iterative development. We further presented GameAnything-Bench, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multimodal reference understanding, game content adaptation, and gameplay quality across diverse game environments. Through evaluations of nine coding agent configurations, we found that current agents can effectively transfer reference content and preserve existing game functionality, but still face challenges in implementing playable interactions and precise modifications. Our results further demonstrate the benefits of multimodal references and iterative refinement, while revealing substantial differences in development capabilities and improvement trajectories across agents. Together, GameAnything and GameAnything-Bench provide unified framework for developing and evaluating inspiration-driven game creation systems, highlighting opportunities for more reliable, adaptable, and autonomous game development. No fixed team can cover every film, novel, place, or play style that people want to bring into games, and no small group of testers can tell us everything that works or breaks on the platform. The counts in this section follow Table A3 and include the commercial candidates of Appendix B.1.2. This set served only as map of popular, moddable genres. We then searched for open-source counterparts genre by genre, matching on genre rather than on individual titles, through the Wikipedia list of open-source games, the bobeff/open-source-games list, osgameclones, GamingOnLinux, and general web search. Within these categories, this first round produced 70 candidates. Because many of these candidates had dated visuals, we ran second search focused on high-quality 3D open-source games, using six parallel web searches totaling about 600 queries. We also included games from our earlier internal tests. In total, 20 games outside the first-round list entered the trial stage: 14 from the 3D searches, 2 tested earlier, 3 from an earlier 2D test, and Minecraft for the commercial track. Selection Requirements Table A3 reports the number of games at each stage. We screened firstround candidates on five requirements: the game runs on our Linux servers without root access, contains real playable content rather than an empty engine, offers modding route such as scripts, data files, level editors, or plugins, has acceptable visuals, and has been maintained since October 2024. Runtime trial. Within these categories, we attempted to deploy 67 games, 57 open-source and the 10 shortlisted commercial games, in Docker sandbox on GPU server, without accounts or logins. Using each games own modding or scripting interface and without patching binaries, we made one or two small visible changes and recorded before-and-after gameplay. Two games could not be deployed: Ryzom Core requires database, web login, and many services, and the data for Arma: Cold War Assault is available only through logged-in Steam account. Manual quality review. We then manually reviewed the recordings of the 65 running games and judged each games overall quality, with visual quality as the primary consideration. Visuals served as minimum bar rather than preference for particular style: 2D and low-polygon games GameAnything were retained when their presentation stayed clear and coherent, while games with the most dated presentation were removed. We also considered overall game quality and complexity, favoring games with enough content and interacting systems to support substantive extension. We also favored games that could show scene at the scale of playable character or world, and removed games dominated by menus, abstract views, or distant map cameras. This step was holistic judgment rather than fixed scoring procedure. It retained 30 games, 25 open-source and 5 commercial; two more were marked as uncertain and did not advance. Development trial. For each of the 25 open-source games, we built four video-adaptation tasks, one each from city, film, game trailer, and sports references, for 100 tasks in total. Each task went through repeated rounds of development, independent playtesting, and independent review; Table A4 shows two of the resulting extensions for each selected game. Final selection. We kept one game per gameplay type by manually comparing the final outputs of these tasks, asking whether the reference content could be clearly expressed in the game. We removed vehicle simulators because their task outputs were weak, and social 3D sandboxes because their gameplay was too thin. The final set requires that code and data can be downloaded without an account, the game can run and be recorded in our GPU sandbox, the game has been successfully modified, the player can take the role of the references protagonist, the game has the strongest visuals in its type, and the selected games cover different kinds of gameplay. Selection Criteria We selected games on three criteria. Popularity: the game has large player base and an active modding community, so its modding interfaces are mature, documented, and widely used. Genre coverage: the selected games span distinct genres and views, so the same reference can be expressed in different ways across games. Modding adaptability: the games modding interface can add the scenes, characters, events, and mechanics that our references call for, rather than only tuning numbers or swapping assets. We also considered runtime cost, since every task requires repeated launches, playtests, and recordings in our GPU sandbox. Games that are very heavy to install and run were deferred for now: The Sims 4 and Grand Theft Auto both carry large installations, require launcher or online components, and are slow to start in our sandbox. Slay the Spire, Civilization VI, Kerbal Space Program, and Overcooked! 2 run well, but their emphasis on card battles, turn-based strategy, spaceflight simulation, and timed cooperative cooking leaves little room for the scenes and stories in our references. We therefore did not select them. We collect multimodal references from diverse sources to cover broad range of creative content. Our video collection includes film clips, gameplay recordings, sports footage, and travel videos. Text references are drawn from novels, short stories, fairy tales, game rules, and descriptions of places and activities. Image references include photographs, paintings, comics, illustrations, and diagrams. The initial collection contains 180 video files, 79 text works, and 77 image groups. We record the source and licensing information of each reference to support traceability and dataset release. Reference Processing and Annotation. We process each modality according to its characteristics while adopting unified annotation scheme, to identify meaningful candidate references. For videos, we remove duplicates, identify relevant clips, and extract timestamped keyframes and transcripts. Two independent annotation passes identify important mechanisms, entities and their properties, and spatial, temporal, and causal relations. For texts, we parse the collected works into passages with stable paragraph references. model examines the source text to identify candidate passages and annotate relevant content with supporting quotations. For images, we group related pictures, detect duplicates, and annotate important visual elements and relationships. These image groups also underwent two independent annotation passes. Across all modalities, annotations are linked to the original evidence through video timestamps, text passages, or image locations. These annotations support task construction but are not provided to the development agents. Candidate Ranking and Human Selection. We score candidate references based on semantic clarity, transfer potential, and evaluation feasibility. For videos, we combine independent model annotations with rule based filtering to obtain candidate shortlist. For texts, Claude identifies and scores candidate passages, while Codex performs comparative ranking to better distinguish candidates with similar scores. For images, model annotations support the identification of important content and redundant references. Human reviewers then inspect the original materials and select the final references, considering both candidate quality and coverage across task categories. The selected GameAnything 36 references are subsequently used to construct benchmark tasks with suitable target games. Table A6 summarizes the collection and selection statistics. The 125 final Construction tasks use 51 distinct videos (74 clips) across the 40 video tasks and 19 hybrid tasks. They use 39 text passages, 30 from 25 public-domain works for the text tasks and nine in hybrid tasks, and 50 image bundles, 36 for the image tasks and 14 in hybrid tasks. These are the final counts in Table A6, and the distribution of the tasks is reported in Table A7. Table A6. Statistics of multimodal reference collection and annotation. sections.content: B.3 Task and Rubric Construction Pilot Calibration and Iterative Rubric Construction. We first calibrate the task construction process on small set of representative tasks through multiple rounds of model generation and human feedback. Based on the feedback, we refine the authoring guidelines, model instructions, and examples before scaling up task generation. For each task, Claude drafts the evaluation rubrics, which are independently checked by Codex for source grounding, scoring consistency, and relevance to the adaptation objective. Claude then reconciles the feedback and revises the rubrics. Every task undergoes human review, where reviewers examine all rubric items and provide feedback until the task is approved. Feedback on individual items leads to targeted revisions, while recurring issues are incorporated into the shared authoring guidelines and applied to other affected tasks. Rubric Authoring Principles. We follow three principles when constructing evaluation rubrics. Each rubric item must be supported by reference evidence or explicit user requirements, with clear scoring anchors for scores of 0, 0.5, and 1. The evaluation criteria focus on the primary transfer objective. Mechanics tasks assess the underlying rules and behaviors, scene tasks emphasize locations and spatial structures, and narrative tasks focus on characters, events, and causal relationships. We avoid requiring incidental details that do not define the intended experience. We apply removal test to determine whether an element is essential: if removing or replacing it preserves the defining rules, setting, or narrative structure, its exact reproduction is not required. This allows different valid implementations without sacrificing the intended reference content. Host Fidelity uses the game-specific checklists described in Appendix C.3, while the executability gate uses the validated capability probes described in Appendix C.1. GameAnything 37 Instruction Construction. Once the rubrics are established, we derive task instructions for Construction and Editing. Construction instructions specify creative goal, requiring agents to realize the reference content in the target game with 2-3 explicit user requests to preserve, specify, and modify content. Editing instructions specify targeted changes to existing entities, properties, mechanisms, or relations, potentially guided by additional references. The corresponding rubrics define both the required modifications and the content that should remain unchanged. All instructions undergo human review and iterative refinement to ensure clarity, feasibility, and alignment with the evaluation criteria. Editing Checkpoint Preparation. We select 31 validated Construction checkpoints as the initial states for 80 Editing tasks, primarily using outputs from Claude Fable 5.2. Each checkpoint must pass executability checks, contain sufficiently complete and playable content, and provide access to the entities or mechanics targeted by the edits. We further verify that the requested changes are not already implemented and that preservation rubrics refer to existing content. All instructions and rubrics are reviewed and revised when necessary. All agents receive the same initial checkpoint for each task, which also serves as the reference for evaluating edit success and preservation. Benchmark Task Distribution. Table A7 reports the distribution of Construction tasks by target game and reference modality. The open-source core contains 77 Construction tasks across nine games, and the commercial track contains 48 tasks across five games, for 125 tasks in total. Table A8 reports the 80 Editing tasks, which start from the checkpoints of 31 Construction tasks with two or three edits each: 64 tasks on six open-source games and 16 on two commercial games. Edits fall into three classes. Appearance modifies the look of existing content in 26 tasks. Content & structure changes objects or spatial layouts in 26 tasks, while behavior & flow modifies rules, parameters, or event sequences in 28 tasks. Most edits target single object, accounting for 61 tasks, while the remaining edits apply to groups of similar objects. The examples cover text, image, video, and hybrid inputs. The hybrid task combines the clip used in the video-only case with separately collected images. sections.content: C.1 Game Capability Probes and Executability Gate Game Capability Probes. Modifications to existing games may break or remove the original game. For each target game, we build executable probes that drive the game through its own inputs and read its state, covering core mechanics, interactions, and system behaviors. We run the same probes on the original and modified games under matched conditions and compare their outcomes. The original game serves as the reference, avoiding the need to manually specify expected states for every capability. Probe Validation. We validate the probes through two complementary tests. First, we perform A/A testing on independent instances of the original game to identify unstable measurements and establish appropriate tolerances. Second, we introduce controlled modifications that deliberately break selected game capabilities and check that only the corresponding probes fail. We exclude probes that cannot be evaluated reliably under the benchmark environment. Executability Gate. The executability gate uses small set of validated probes for each game, as listed in Table A15. These include common stability probe and two checks that the original playable content remains accessible. These probes do not penalize intended changes such as new content or modified values; submission fails only if it crashes, produces new errors, or removes or replaces the original game wholesale. The gate uses 27 probes across the nine open-source games and 15 probes across the five commercial games. Host Fidelity separately assesses whether the new experience uses the target games original environment and systems, as detailed in Appendix C.3. Table A15. Executability gate probes. games and 15 on the five commercial games with Stable counted once per game C.2 Agent Execution and Independent Evaluation Agent Execution and Submission. Each agent receives the reference materials, the task instruction, the target game, and per-game development kit. Execution is single stage with development budget of 120 minutes of wall-clock time per task, within which the agent analyzes the references, implements the modification, and tests it in the running game. Agents interact with the game through shared command-line interface that builds the modification, starts fresh game, sends keyboard and mouse input, captures screenshots, reads the structured game state, and replays input traces. The run ends when the agent marks its submission as complete or the budget is exhausted; an agent that stops early without marking completion is asked to continue. Each task runs in its own Docker container built from an image pinned by digest, with fresh game instance and no network access. Agents run inside these containers using Claude Code, Codex CLI, or OpenCode with their default prompts and tools. Model requests leave the container only through host-side proxy that attaches the credentials, so no credential is visible to the agent. Failures of the environment rather than the agent, such as an unavailable container or model API error, are detected and classified automatically; the affected task is rerun and is not scored as an agent failure. The final submission includes the game modification, gameplay traces, screenshots, and instructions for accessing the created content. We freeze the submitted artifacts and evaluate them in separate, clean game instance. This separation prevents temporary development states from affecting the evaluation. Action Replay and Independent Agent Playtesting. We employ two complementary methods to evaluate the implemented functions and gameplay experience. Action Replay executes the player actions submitted by the development agent, while Independent Agent Playtesting actively explores the modified game. Let 𝐺 denote the modified game and 𝐴sub the submitted action sequence. The replay trace is obtained by 𝜏rep = Execute(𝐺, 𝐴sub). For independent playtesting, an evaluation agent with policy 𝜋eval interacts with the same modified game: (9) 𝜏play Interact(𝐺, 𝜋eval). (10) GameAnything 48 Action Replay verifies the functions demonstrated by the development agent. The evaluator reexecutes the submitted actions in clean game instance and records the resulting observations. Independent Agent Playtesting further examines the game without relying solely on these demonstrations. It first explores the game without access to the developers traces or navigation instructions. In second stage, it receives the submitted traces and access instructions to verify specific functions and investigate potential failures. This allows the evaluator to assess both demonstrated functionality and behaviors encountered through independent exploration. Each playtest is limited to 40 actions and 30 minutes; the judge may stop earlier once it has the evidence it needs. Appendix H.3 shows that agreement with human labels stops improving beyond 30 to 40 actions. Evidence Collection and Adjudication. Both evaluators collect screenshots and runtime game states during interaction. Screenshots provide evidence of visual outcomes and spatial arrangements, while state changes help verify functional behaviors. For mechanisms and narrative events, we examine whether player actions produce the expected state transitions. This helps distinguish functional implementations from static visual demonstrations. Runtime states are read as structured JSON containing the engine fields listed in Table A16, content added by the modification, and on-screen text. Every replay and playtest screenshot is paired with state snapshot, allowing the judge to compare the effects of actions. For Tanks of Freedom II and Cities: Skylines, which lack directly controlled avatar, state changes in buildings, units, resources, or game time provide much of the functional evidence and must agree with the screenshots. For visual evaluation, vision judge compares screenshots of the generated content against the corresponding reference evidence and task rubrics. The comparison focuses on semantic and visual characteristics rather than exact reproduction, allowing different visual styles across target games. Candidate screenshots come from the action replay and the independent playtest, both captured by the evaluator in clean game instance; for each rubric item, the judge selects the screenshots that best show the item before scoring it. The replay and playtesting evaluators independently score each rubric item. When their judgments agree, the score is accepted directly. Otherwise, an additional judge examines the supporting evidence and scoring criteria to resolve the disagreement. We record the initial judgments and adjudication results; Appendix H.2 reports how often the verifiers agree and how adjudication changes the scores. C.3 Scoring Rules and Aggregation Rubric Scoring and Executability Gate. Construction is evaluated on Content, Functions & Playability, Visual & Presentation, and Host Fidelity; Editing on Edit Success, Preservation, and Host Fidelity. Each rubric item includes explicit scoring criteria and supporting evidence. Rubric items use three scoring levels of 0, 0.5, and 1; Host Fidelity is also scored 0, 0.5, or 1, derived from per-game host-feature checklist as described below. We assign equal importance to all applicable rubric items within each dimension and do not use additional critical item penalties. Before evaluation, we check whether the submitted modification can be built, installed, and loaded in clean game instance, and the gate probes of Appendix C.1 check that the game stays stable and that the original game is still present. The two task settings share the same evaluation dimensions but differ in their scoring objectives. For Construction, the Content, Functions & Playability, and Visual & Presentation rubrics assess how well the generated game realizes the reference materials and user instructions, while Host Fidelity checks whether the adaptation is built on and played through the target game. For Editing, Edit Success items check whether the requested change to content, behavior, or appearance is realized; an item that cannot be tested from the evidence counts as zero. Preservation items compare the edited game against its initial checkpoint to detect unintended changes to content and functions the edit should not touch; items that do not apply to the edit are excluded. Host Fidelity uses the same per-game checklist as in Construction. The Editing Overall calculation, including penalties for failures in Preservation and Host Fidelity, is specified below. Host Fidelity Scoring. Host Fidelity assesses whether the created experience builds upon the original game rather than replacing its world and systems with an independent implementation. sections.title: G Additional Ablations and Robustness Analysis
sections.content: G.1 Shared Task Subset and Protocol Both analyses use the same 40-task Construction subset, spanning open-source and commercial games, all four input modalities, and the three task categories. Each task contains rubric criteria that depend on information in the references but not the task instruction. We evaluate submissions with the Lite protocol and compute paired bootstrap confidence intervals over tasks. G.2 Reference Ablation Multimodal references provide information that task instructions alone cannot recover. We test this by withholding the references while keeping the task instructions and evaluation unchanged. On the subset of 40 tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 loses 7.1 Overall points in comparison using the same harness version. The decline is concentrated in Content and Visual & Presentation, while Functions & Playability shows no clear change. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, compared against its main run, declines on all dimensions, including Functions & Playability (16.7). These results support the benchmarks focus on development grounded in external references rather than instruction following alone. Table A27 reports the full ablation results. G.3 Variance across Development Runs Individual development outcomes vary substantially across attempts, while aggregate model comparisons are more stable. We repeat Claude Sonnet 5.5 development on the same 40 tasks with independent seeds and the same 120-minute budget. The two additional runs share harness version, whereas the original main run used an earlier version, so differences across all three runs cannot be attributed entirely to randomness. Across the two comparable runs, the mean standard deviation per task is 7.6 points. Nevertheless, Sonnet ranks second on the subset in all three runs. Its margin over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash changes considerably, indicating that small differences between agents should be interpreted cautiously. Table A28 reports the run-level comparisons. sections.title: H Evaluation Reliability Analysis
sections.content: The following analyses complement Section 7.4 by examining agreement with human judgments, the value of evaluation evidence, and stability across repeated runs and judge families. We call the replay verifier Lite and the protocol combining replay, independent playtesting, and adjudication Full. Human comparisons cover Content, Functions & Playability, and Visual & Presentation because annotators did not score Host Fidelity. Unless otherwise noted, scores use 0 to 100 scale and confidence intervals are computed from 4,000 bootstrap resamples over submissions. H.1 Agreement with Human Judgments The Full evaluator closely matches human judgments and preserves comparisons among models. We evaluate 40 frozen submissions from six agent models, with two human annotators using the same rubrics and gameplay evidence. Full achieves Pearson correlation of 𝑟 = 0.87 and mean absolute error of 8.8 points, and it reproduces the human ranking of all six models exactly. At the GameAnything 59 rubric level, 71% of items receive the same score, with few disagreements at opposite extremes. These results support aggregate agent comparisons while leaving room for error on individual submissions. Figure 7 and Table A29 provide the detailed comparisons. Table A29. Agent-model ranking. Mean overall score, 0100, and rank of each agent model on the 40 human-labeled trials under human labels, the Full judge, and three judge families re-scoring the same saved evidence. Shaded ranks differ from the human ranking. Spearman correlation with the human ranking: Full judge 1.00, Claude 0.94, Codex 0.94, Gemini 0.94.

GameAnything: User Interface and Workflow Section 4 describes how GameAnything develops game; this appendix expands Section 4.3 and describes how user works with it. GameAnything ships as skill compatible with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and other coding agents, together with local web application. The user starts project with one sentence to the agent; from then on all interaction happens in the browser, and the user never edits code. Layout. The web application runs on the users own machine and is bound to the local host, as shown in Figure A3. Each page has three parts: project sidebar with the list of versions and rounds, conversation with the agent, and workspace with tabs for materials, scenes or personal memories, characters, planning, gameplay, development status, and taking home the result. The agent and the interface share state only through files in the project folder: an append-only conversation log, review GameAnything files written by the pages, and the plan and status files that the pages render. Every page reads these files on each request, so project can be closed, exported, or reopened at any point, and finished project can be exported as read-only demo that replays every page. Figure A3. The GameAnything web application for Dream of the Red Chamber in Minecraft. The left panel lists projects and rounds, the center shows an agent conversation, and the right displays extracted scenes with source evidence, grounding status, and editable review controls. Project steps appear across the top. Cards instead of open questions. The agent asks for decisions through structured cards rather than open-ended questions, as illustrated in Figure A4. An understanding card lists what the agent took from the material and lets the user edit any line before confirming. An options card offers lettered choices with recommended default and short note on cost or consequence; candidates card offers generated preview pictures or sounds to pick from, or to reject with reason; questions card gathers facts that only the user knows. permission card states what will be sent to which model and what will not, and its estimated cost, before any of the users material leaves the machine; each request is logged. go card states the scope of version, its budget of playtest rounds and hours, and its estimated cost, and nothing is built until the user starts it. result card reports delivered version with the users chosen preview next to the final in-game screenshot. Only the users click marks step as confirmed; the agent cannot confirm on the users behalf, and every answer can be changed later. Four modes. Projects follow four modes, each with defined sequence of steps listed in Table A31. Steps that need the users decision are never skipped, and each such step sends its card in the same turn. The agent prepares extraction, designs, and plans; the user confirms them, approves every permission and paid generation, starts each version, and decides what happens after it. In the adaptation mode, copyright step records whether the source is in the public domain: only GameAnything Figure A4. Decision cards from Dream of the Red Chamber and Hong Kong food project. Each delivered version includes recorded playtest divided into chapters for individual places or scenes, as shown in panel of Figure A5. For each chapter the play page shows the in-game frame and the approved target picture side by side, the reviewers checks, which the user may override, and buttons to accept the moment or request changes. Feedback is anchored to evidence: comment is saved with its time and the current video frame, box can be drawn on the frame to mark spot, and an image can be attached; moment can also be sent into the conversation with its frame. Each piece of feedback becomes record that keeps the users own words, the agents interpretation, and the anchor; when the agent is unsure what the user meant, it asks back with the frame before changing anything. After fix, the same anchor is shot again and shown next to the earlier frame, and the record is closed only when the user accepts it. The user closes the review by marking the version fine or by handing the collected notes to the next version. Progress and status. The development status page renders the persistent state described in Section 4.1, as shown in panel of Figure A5. It displays each requests status, verification evidence, unresolved issues, and items to recheck. Statuses include done, partly done, to do, broken, and regressed. It is read-only; changes are requested in the conversation. During development, the work view in panel of Figure A5 shows the current activity, round, time budget, and latest screenshots so that users can monitor progress. live, view-only picture of the game is available after separate permission. If the build stalls, hits usage limit, or needs login, single status line says so in the conversation together with the expected reset time. Running and installing. project builds either in sandbox, container on the users machine or server with the game, its mod loader, and build tools, or natively on the users own copy of the game. In native mode the agent opens the game only after the user agrees or within time window the user chooses, never takes the window focus, and closes only what it opened. The take-home page installs finished version into the users own game in five steps; all saves are backed up first, only the games mods folder changes, and every install can be undone. Preferences learned from user feedback, as GameAnything 65 described in Section 4.2, appear on separate page where each entry can be edited, disabled, or deleted. New entries are used only after the user enables them. GameAnything: Iterative Development Case Studies This section illustrates the GameAnything iteration process described in Section 4 through three longer projects. Hogwarts from the Harry Potter novels and the Grand View Garden from Dream of the Red Chamber were built as Minecraft mods. Five places on the San Diego coast were built in Cities: Skylines using the users photos and public images. Each project went through several versions. Within each version, the builder and an independent critic alternate as described in Section 4.1. The critic tests the current build against approved targets and identifies concrete issues for the builder to fix. Between versions, the user provides sparse feedback through text and annotated video frames, sometimes extending the scope to new rooms, characters, or landmarks. In total, Hogwarts took 4 versions with 21 critic rounds, the Grand View Garden 6 versions with 28 critic rounds, and San Diego 3 phases with 12 logged critic playtests. Tables A32A35 trace these projects from the source material to the final build. Each column follows one place from the same viewpoint, and each row is one round, so reading column from top to bottom shows how the place changes; the text above each row summarizes the critics findings, the builders changes, and the users feedback at that point, and frames with an amber border are the users own annotated feedback. The critics findings catch problems that single development pass leaves behind, such as flat facades, empty rooms, floating blocks, or actors placed below the floor, while the users feedback adds what the critic cannot judge, such as which places should feel crowded or which landmarks are missing. Over the rounds, the number of places the critic judges close to their targets rises in both Minecraft projects, and in San Diego the critics total score for the five places rises from 15 to 27 out of 50 in the first phase.
